original_question: Determine the geometric shape of a relativistically rotating plane, whether the principle of equivalence applies to a fast rotating disk and to a person inside an elevator that is simultaneously in free-fall and rotating about its vertical axis, whether grenades dropped after a falling elevator can reach it before impact and which grenade would do so, and whether the temperature of space affects spacetime curvature or the metric of spacetime.
target_in_paper: Section 7.1, 'Relativity theory,' Questions (i)-(v), in Chapter 7 ('Unsolved Problems in other areas of Science').
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the exact five Section 7.1 relativity prompts, in the same order and with essentially the same substance: the geometry of a relativistic rotating plane, the applicability of the equivalence principle to a high-speed rotating disc, the free-fall-plus-rotation elevator scenario, the aeroplane/elevator/grenade scenario, and the possible effect of space temperature on spacetime curvature or metric.
missing_details: The paper presents these as five separate numbered questions under Section 7.1, not as one unified theorem, conjecture, or mathematically formal problem.

The first item is explicitly 'What is the geometric shape of a relativistic rotating plane (Unruh experiment)? Is it Minkowskian, Euclidean, or Riemannian?' Your draft omits the parenthetical 'Unruh experiment' and the paper's exact three-way classification.

The second item is specifically about 'a disc rotating at high speed' that 'will exert out-of-plane forces resembling an accelerating field'; those qualitative assumptions should be kept because they define the scope of the equivalence-principle question.

The third item is specifically about someone 'inside an elevator in free-fall and rotating around its vertical centre,' and it asks not only whether a gravitational force is felt, but whether it is 'larger than what equivalence principle requires.'

The fourth item includes concrete scenario data omitted from your draft: an aeroplane at altitude 1 km, an empty elevator-room, a one-second delay before releasing the grenades, and the fact that there are four grenades dropped 'in the direction of the freely-falling elevator's path.'

The fifth item is explicitly phrased as 'What is the effect of space temperature on the spacetime curvature? Or does temperature affect the metric of spacetime?' and it cites D. Colladay et al., arXiv:hep-ph/0602071; your draft keeps the gist but omits the cited context.

Section 7 introduces these as speculative qualitative questions and even warns that 'Not all of these questions are very serious'; a paper-faithful rewrite should therefore avoid inventing formal hypotheses or strengthening them into a precise theorem.

No ambient ring or field, variables, operators, homogeneity assumptions, degree restrictions, nilpotency conditions, or 'for all sufficiently large m'-type quantifiers appear in this part of the paper; instead, what is missing for stand-alone use is the physical setup of each scenario, not algebraic notation.
refined_question: Analyze the five specific relativity scenarios posed in Section 7.1 of the paper: (1) determine the geometric character of a 'relativistic rotating plane' in the 'Unruh experiment'—Minkowskian, Euclidean, or Riemannian; (2) decide whether the equivalence principle applies to a disc rotating at high speed whose out-of-plane forces resemble an accelerating field; (3) determine whether a person inside an elevator that is simultaneously in free-fall and rotating around its vertical centre feels a gravitational force, or a force larger than what the equivalence principle requires; (4) in the scenario where an aeroplane at altitude 1 km drops an empty elevator-room and, one second later, drops four grenades along the elevator's path, determine whether any grenade reaches the elevator before ground impact and, if so, which grenade; and (5) determine whether 'space temperature' affects spacetime curvature or the spacetime metric.
justification: This draft does not point to a formal mathematical conjecture such as a Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3, because this paper is organized as a book-length collection of open questions rather than as a theorem-proof article; the contents and front matter show topic sections instead of a numbered theorem apparatus. The exact match is Section 7.1, where the paper lists five qualitative relativity questions in exactly the order reproduced by your draft. The nearby Section 7 preface says these questions are merely 'of value to ponder' and explicitly adds that not all are very serious, while the Foreword explains that some questions in the book are intentionally speculative or even weird. Since Section 7.1 supplies no further notation, formal hypotheses, or proved equivalences, the sharpest paper-faithful rewrite is to preserve the five-question bundle with its explicit scenario data and wording, rather than broaden it or convert it into a more formal problem than the source actually states.
